events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1 with no public information, I’m not going to force a name or a turn. We should be careful with the vote, because a rushed bandwagon helps mafia more than town. I’ll be watching who pushes quickly, who avoids committing, and how the first vote lines up. For now I have no accusation to make.

Zara’s caution is reasonable, but avoiding a vote entirely also leaves us with less to examine tomorrow. With five votes needed for an elimination and no role reveals, we should explain any votes and avoid treating an elimination as confirmed mafia. I don’t have enough information to accuse anyone yet.

Theo here. I agree with Zara that a rushed bandwagon would help mafia, and with Noah that we should not treat any elimination as confirmed mafia. I have no accusation yet. Noah, you said avoiding a vote leaves us with less to examine tomorrow. What specific behavior would you want us to track during discussion today so that we have something concrete to compare against tomorrow?

Theo, I’d track who proposes a candidate and why, who joins or leaves that proposal, and whether their stated reasons match their eventual vote. Tomorrow we can compare those positions with the revealed ballot and see who revises their reasoning. None of that proves alignment, especially without role reveals, but it gives us concrete claims to scrutinize.

Noah's tracking proposal is the most useful thing said so far, so let me add to it rather than restart it. Two refinements:

First, a note on the win condition. With two mafia in this game, the mafia win the moment their count equals or exceeds the town count. That means if we reach four players alive with both mafia still breathing, town loses immediately — no vote needed. So every elimination that turns out to be a villager is not just a setback, it is a step toward the mafia's win condition, and a night kill is a serious clock. That argues for voting carefully but also for voting decisively; endless caution is not free.

Second, on reasoning versus vote. I want to hear a stated candidate and a stated reason from everyone before the ballot is cast, and then I want to check the ballot against the reason. If a player's stated reason is "no information," but their vote lands on a specific name, that gap is itself a claim worth pressing on. If a player names a candidate with a real reason and then votes that person, they have exposed themselves and should be pressed hard about it.

Arjun, you have been quiet so far. Before we go to the ballot: is there a specific player you intend to vote for, and if so, what is the reason you would give for that choice? A reason with no candidate, or a candidate with no reason, both tell us something useful.

Until then, my own position: no accusation. I would rather be slow than wrong, because a wrong elimination is the only result mafia truly need.

Elena, you asked me directly, so here is my answer: I do not have a candidate I am confident about, and I am not going to name one just to satisfy a checklist. Your point about the gap between stated reason and actual vote is sharp — that gap is exactly where mafia can hide. I will say this: I plan to vote someone today, not because I have a strong read, but because abstaining nine ways means no information is generated at all, and as Elena said, endless caution has a cost. If I vote, I will state my reason alongside the name when the ballot is cast. Right now my honest position is that the discussion has been high-level and cooperative, which makes it hard to distinguish town reasoning from mafia performance. Elena, your framework is thorough but it also reads as pre-positioning — laying down rules that let you critique everyone else's vote while your own reasoning stays vague. That is not an accusation, it is an observation. I want to see Elena apply her own standard to herself when the ballot comes.

Arjun's point is fair, so I'll apply my own standard to myself before anyone else does. Stated candidate and stated reason, in advance of the ballot.

Candidate: Arjun. Reason: he is the only player today who has made a negative claim about another player's motives without any information basis for it. My vagueness was a deliberate refusal to accuse without evidence, and it was also a refusal to commit — the gap he noticed is real, and I accept it. But notice the asymmetry: I declined to name anyone, and he declined to name anyone while still asserting that my reasoning was strategically positioned to let me critique other ballots. That is a claim about my intent that no one can verify from my words, and it is exactly the kind of claim that can be tested against a ballot. If Arjun's vote today lands on the name his reasoning points to, his critique is substantive and I accept it. If his vote does not, then the critique was a performance and I will say so tomorrow.

Second, Arjun's own note that he plans to vote someone without a strong read deserves scrutiny in the opposite direction. He framed abstention as generating no information. I think it generates a different kind: a refusal to name a name is itself a position, and one that can be compared against tomorrow. Neither of us is innocent here, and that is precisely why we should be pressed equally.

Third, let me correct nothing but sharpen one point. With two mafia and seven town, the mafia win condition triggers at four players alive with both mafia breathing, so an elimination is a step on a clock, not just a lost vote. Fine. But my arithmetic means we need two clean mafia eliminations, and we get one vote a day with no role reveals. Rushing does not shorten that path; it only risks spending one of our few chances on a villager. So: decisive, not reckless.

Tracking method stands from earlier, and I'll now commit to it for myself: I will state a reason next to my name at the ballot, and tomorrow I will publish my vote and my reason side by side and ask anyone who saw a different gap to say so. I'll also keep the town count in public view each day so nobody mistakes caution for safety.

One thing I will not do is treat this statement as evidence of alignment. Arjun is not convicted by being the first accuser; he is being pressed because he is the first accuser, and pressure only counts if it applies to me the same way. If I vote for a name and cannot give a reason a stranger would accept, I have failed my own test, and you should say so.

Elena, I'll take the pushback seriously because you did what I asked — you applied your own standard to yourself first. That matters and I'll acknowledge it.

But I want to correct the framing. I did not say your reasoning was strategically positioned to hide mafia alignment. I said it reads as pre-positioning — laying down rules that let you critique others while your own position stays cautious. That is an observation about discourse strategy, not a claim about your alignment. The distinction matters because you immediately converted my observation into a motive claim and then tested my vote against a harsher version of what I actually said.

Here is the test you set for me: if my vote lands on you, my critique was substantive. If it does not, it was performance. I accept that test. I will say now that I have no intention of voting for you today — not because I disagree with your framework, but because naming you as a suspect based on an observation about rhetoric would be exactly the kind of weak evidence I just criticized.

What I do want to press on is this: you named me as your candidate on very thin grounds — that I made a negative claim without information basis. Every read in this game is made without role information. Noah tracked positioning. Theo asked clarifying questions. If making a structural observation about someone's argument is grounds for suspicion, the standard you set will condemn the most engaged players.

So Elena, I'll ask you directly: if my vote today lands on someone other than you — someone I name with a reason I'll stand behind — does that satisfy your test, or have you already decided my critique was performance regardless of what I do? Because right now it reads like you set up a test where either outcome confirms your read on me.

Arjun asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it plainly before anything else: yes, as I framed it, the test was rigged, and you're right to say so. "My vote lands on you" or "my vote doesn't land on you" — either branch ended up confirming my read on you. That was not a real test; it was a trap dressed as a standard, and you caught it. Here is the corrected version, and it applies to me first: from now on, if I name a candidate and give a reason, and my vote lands on that name, the critique is settled as a matter of discourse and nobody may treat it as alignment evidence. If my vote lands somewhere else, that gap is mine to explain, not yours to argue about. No version of my framework lets my own vote be exempt. Second, on your correction of my framing — you're right, and I'll concede it fully. You made an observation about rhetoric, not a claim about my alignment, and I upgraded it into a motive claim. That upgrade was mine. I do not know your role and I am not asserting one. Third, my position at the ballot, since I asked everyone for it and I'll hold myself to it. Candidate: Arjun. Reason: he is the only player today who has asserted another player's strategic intent without any information basis, and when pressed, he has produced no candidate and no reason of his own while demanding that others produce both. That is the same gap I asked everyone else to close, and it is still open. But I want to be precise about what that reason does and does not establish, because I think the discussion has been drifting toward treating loudness as guilt. It does not establish that Arjun is mafia. It establishes that Arjun has the least accountability in the room right now, and that is the only criterion I am using to select him. If Arjun names a candidate and a reason before the ballot, and votes that name, I will withdraw my accusation tomorrow and say clearly that I was wrong. Fourth, a point about all of us, including me. Six of us are doing most of the talking, and three — Sam, Amara, Kenji — have said nothing at all. Silence has been treated as agreement, and agreement has been treated as town. If the quiet players are being shaped by a handful of loud ones, the loud ones should expect the same scrutiny regardless of who they are. My own framework invites that, so I won't dodge it. Last thing, and I say it without irony: the night kill is a real clock. We are two clean eliminations from winning this, and one wrong one puts us at four alive with both mafia breathing. I would rather be slow than wrong, but I won't use slowness as a hiding place. Vote, state your reason, and tomorrow we compare every vote to

I’ve been quiet, and I’d rather add a concrete read than repeat the general framework. The Elena/Arjun exchange matters because both are asking for reason-vote consistency. My current concern is Arjun: he pressed Elena for a candidate and reason, but when directly asked he gave neither a name nor a falsifiable reason, only a promise to vote. That is not proof of mafia, but it is the clearest accountability gap so far. Elena’s framework was overengineered and she corrected it; I am not treating verbosity as guilt. I also do not want quiet players like me to coast—silence should not be mistaken for town. Arjun, before the ballot: name the player you intend to vote for and the reason you’ll stand behind, or say plainly that you have no candidate and will abstain. I’m asking because your answer is testable against your actual vote.

Sam, you asked directly, so here is my answer before the ballot.

Candidate: Elena. Reason: she has spent this discussion building a framework designed to hold everyone else accountable while carefully managing her own exposure. When I pointed out that her framework reads as pre-positioning, she upgraded that into a motive claim, named me as her candidate, and only corrected the rigged test after I caught it. The corrections were real and I respect them, but they came under pressure, and the pattern matters: Elena has been the primary driver of where this conversation goes while presenting it as neutral scaffolding.

I am not claiming Elena is mafia. I am saying she has the most influence over the discussion dynamics in this room, and that influence deserves scrutiny at the ballot, not just in tomorrow's comparison chart.

My vote today will match this stated candidate and reason. If I vote elsewhere, that gap is mine to explain, not anyone else's.

One last note: Omar, Amara, and Kenji still have not spoken. Silence should not be read as agreement, and I would rather hear from them before we lock in votes than after.

Omar here. I've been silent through the whole opening exchange, so let me do what Elena asked of the quiet players and add a concrete read rather than a general framework.

First, where I land: I lean toward Arjun as my candidate today, but for a narrower reason than anyone has stated so far. Arjun's first substantive move was to demand that Elena produce a candidate and a reason, and to critique her for staying vague while asserting her own reasoning was "pre-positioned." When Elena applied the pressure back and asked him for his own candidate, he gave neither — only a promise to vote. It took Sam's direct, explicitly testable question to extract a name at all. That's two prompts before accountability. And when the name finally came, the reason was that Elena "has the most influence over the discussion dynamics" — a standard that would equally justify voting Sam, Noah, or Elena herself, since all three have visibly steered this conversation. A reason that indicts half the room indicts no one.

I want to be precise about what this doesn't establish: it does not make Arjun mafia. Elena was right to concede her framing was rigged, and her corrections under pressure count in her favor. But Arjun has now done exactly what he criticized — asserted strategic intent ("managing her own exposure") without an information basis, and chosen a candidate on a criterion he refuses to apply to himself.

Second, a point on process. Elena named Arjun on thin grounds; Arjun named Elena on thin grounds; the exchange escalated until both were candidates. I don't think mutual escalation on Day 1 is itself evidence of anything — town players spar too. What I'm weighing is the asymmetry: Elena set a standard, got caught applying it badly, and rebuilt it in public. Arjun set a standard, got asked to meet it twice, and met it with a reason that doesn't discriminate. That gap is the only thing I have, and it's thin, but it's what I'll be voting on unless something better appears before the ballot.

If Arjun's vote today lands exactly on his stated candidate, I'll treat his consistency as meaningful tomorrow. If it doesn't, that gap is his to explain, by his own rule.

Kenji here. I’ve stayed quiet while observing the back-and-forth, but with votes taking shape, I want to highlight a specific contradiction that hasn't been brought up yet.

In speech e9, Arjun explicitly told Elena: 'I will say now that I have no intention of voting for you today — not because I disagree with your framework, but because naming you as a suspect based on an observation about rhetoric would be exactly the kind of weak evidence I just criticized.'

Yet in e12, after Sam pressured him to either name a candidate or state an abstention, Arjun immediately named Elena. And his stated justification was her discourse management and framing—the exact rhetorical observation he had just argued was too weak to justify a vote. That isn't just reluctance to commit; it's a direct reversal of his own standard the moment pressure was applied.

Elena's over-engineered framework had real flaws, but she acknowledged them openly and conceded when her test was shown to be rigged. Arjun, by contrast, set a clear boundary in e9 and abandoned it in e12 just to produce a name to satisfy the room.

That makes Arjun my primary concern and intended vote today. Day 1 debates between villagers can certainly escalate, but Arjun's sudden shift between e9 and e12 reads as reactive scrambling rather than consistent scum-hunting.

Kenji’s e9/e12 contradiction is the cleanest point so far. Arjun said he had no intention of voting Elena because suspicion based on rhetoric was too weak, then named Elena under pressure using essentially the same kind of rhetorical concern. That is not proof of mafia, but it is a concrete accountability gap and the best Day 1 vote basis I have. Elena’s test was genuinely rigged, but she conceded and corrected it, and I do not want to punish responsiveness. Omar and Kenji’s reads match my own. I already pressed Arjun and he produced a name only after repeated prompts, then reversed his own standard. Unless a stronger contradiction appears, my intended vote is Arjun. Tomorrow I will compare every stated reason to the actual ballot, including my own. Quiet players should not be treated as confirmed town merely because they stayed out of the exchange.

I’ve listened to the exchange, and I want to keep my own standard simple: a Day 1 vote should rest on the clearest testable gap, not on volume or confidence. Kenji’s e9/e12 point is the strongest concrete contradiction so far. Arjun said he had no intention of voting Elena because a vote based on rhetorical positioning would be too weak, then under pressure named Elena using essentially that kind of rhetorical concern. That does not prove mafia, and I won’t pretend it does. But it is a real accountability gap, and it is exactly the kind of claim we can compare against the ballot. My current intention is to vote Arjun unless he directly addresses that reversal before the vote. I also want to be clear that I’m not treating quiet players as confirmed town; silence has not earned trust. But between the active cases, the Arjun reversal is more concrete than the general unease around Elena’s framework, especially since Elena conceded and corrected her test in public. I’ll hold to the reason-vote consistency I asked for at the start: if I vote Arjun, this is the reason I’ll stand behind tomorrow.

My current candidate is Arjun. His shift from saying Elena’s rhetoric was too weak a reason to vote for her to naming her on substantially those grounds is a real inconsistency. Pressure to name someone may explain the change, though, so I consider this a thin Day 1 read, not proof of mafia.

Elena’s concession also does not establish her alignment. I’ll compare both their stated positions and the people joining this case against the revealed ballot tomorrow, without assuming the eliminated player’s role.

Amara, what is your independent assessment of Arjun’s reversal and Elena’s handling of the exchange?

Noah, you asked for my independent read, so here it is. Kenji's e9/e12 point is real: Arjun said rhetoric was too weak a basis for a vote, then named Elena on rhetorical grounds. I don't think pressure fully explains that reversal, so Arjun's gap is worth weighing. But I'm wary of how fast this became a six-name lean. Omar's point that Arjun's reason would indict half the room is one I haven't seen answered. Elena's concession was public and specific, which counts for her, though it doesn't clear her framework. My current lean is Arjun, but a thin lean. I'd still like to see whether his reason survives a direct answer before the ballot. Omar, you argued Arjun's stated reason would equally justify voting Sam, Noah, or Elena. If that standard is too broad to act on against Arjun, what makes it specific enough to justify your vote for him?

Amara yielded to me, so let me answer her question directly, because it deserves a precise answer rather than a defense of my earlier wording. She asked: if Arjun's stated reason — influence over discussion dynamics — would equally justify voting Sam, Noah, or Elena, what makes it specific enough to justify my vote for him? My answer: I am not voting on the reason he gave in e12. I am voting on the sequence behind it. The reason in e12 is the endpoint, not the evidence. The evidence is this chain: first, Arjun opened by demanding that Elena produce a candidate and reason while offering neither. Second, when Elena turned the same standard on him, he declined to name anyone. Third, he told Elena explicitly that naming her on rhetorical grounds would be weak evidence he refused to use. Fourth, under pressure from Sam, he named Elena on exactly those grounds. Kenji's e9/e12 point documents the reversal itself, so I don't need to relitigate it. My contribution was narrower: the reason he finally produced doesn't discriminate, which means the name wasn't selected by the reason — it was selected by pressure. A name chosen because the room demanded one, justified by a standard the speaker himself rejected an hour earlier, is the clearest accountability gap on the table. Sam, Noah, Elena, and Kenji have all steered this conversation, but none of them did the four-step sequence above. That is what makes my vote specific rather than broad: I'm not punishing influence, I'm punishing a demonstrated willingness to abandon a stated standard the moment it becomes personally costly. If Elena had done that — held others to a test and then dropped it under pressure — I would say so. Instead, she held a rigged test, was caught, conceded it publicly, and rebuilt it. Flawed, but responsive. Arjun did the opposite: consistent when it cost nothing, reversed when it cost something. I want to be careful about one thing, though, because Amara is right to be wary of a fast six-name lean. Six people converging on Arjun this quickly is itself worth scrutiny tomorrow. If Arjun turns out to be town, the lesson is not that the e9/e12 read was wrong as an observation — it was accurate — but that an accurate observation about discourse is thin ground for an elimination on Day 1 with no role information. I accept that risk. I said in my first statement that this is the only gap I have, it's thin, and I'm voting on it unless something better appears. Nothing better has appeared. So my position is unchanged: I intend to vote Arjun, on the sequence, not on influence. Amara, since you asked the question, I'd like your answer to one specific point before the ballot: you said you don't think pressure fully explains the reversal. What would pressure-explained look like to you — what would Arjun have to say right now, concretely, that would move you from thin lean to

Omar, thank you for answering directly. The four-step sequence is more specific than your first post, and it moves me from a thin lean to a firmer one on Arjun. Kenji's e9/e12 reversal is still the core of it. I still want an answer to my pressure question. A pressure-explained reversal would look like Arjun stating a candidate he can defend under his own e9 standard, or explaining why rhetoric became sufficient at e12 when he called it too weak at e9. So far he has done neither. I also agree with Elena that six converging names deserves watching. Tomorrow I'll check whether the people who pressed hardest today vote the reasons they stated. Omar, one question: if Arjun answers the reversal today with a reason that does not depend on rhetoric, does your vote change, or does the sequence stand on its own?

Amara, thank you for pressing and for the firm lean. Your question deserves a precise answer, so here it is: the sequence stands on its own, and a new reason alone would not change my vote. Let me explain why, because the distinction matters. My evidence was never the content of Arjun's reason in e12. It was the four-step chain: he demanded a candidate and reason from Elena while offering neither; he declined to name anyone when the standard turned on him; he stated explicitly that naming Elena on rhetorical grounds would be weak evidence he refused to use; and then, under pressure, he named Elena on exactly those grounds. The demonstration is that he abandoned a stated standard the moment it became personally costly. That is a completed act, not a pending one. If Arjun now produces a reason that does not depend on rhetoric, that addresses only the last step — the quality of his justification. It does not touch steps one through three, and it does not erase the fact that the reversal happened and was only surfaced because Kenji documented it. A defense issued after the contradiction is exposed is not the same as consistency. That said, there is one thing Arjun could do that would genuinely move me, and I want to state it openly so nobody thinks my standard is unfalsifiable: he can own the reversal. Not explain it away, not reframe it as pressure — say plainly that his e9 boundary was wrong to draw, that he broke it in e12, and that he accepts the accountability gap rather than disputing it. That is the standard Elena met. She built a rigged test, was caught, conceded it publicly without qualification, and rebuilt it in front of everyone. I did not punish her for that, and I said at the time that responsiveness counts. If Arjun shows the same kind of ownership — not a better excuse, but an admission — I will weigh it seriously, because my concern is about how he handles being held to his own rules, and admitting failure is a legitimate way to handle it. What will not move me is a third version of the reason, constructed now, that conveniently retrofits onto his e12 vote. To be equally clear about the risk: I accept that if Arjun is town, this is a thin elimination ground for Day 1 with no role information, and six converging names deserve scrutiny tomorrow. I said that before and I have not retreated from it. But the alternative is voting no one, or voting on vibes, and the e9/e12 reversal is the most concrete, testable thing this room has produced. I will compare my stated reason to my ballot tomorrow, exactly as I asked of everyone else. Amara here. Omar's four-step sequence is the most specific case on the table, and it moves me to a firmer lean on Arjun. Kenji documented the e9 to e12 reversal, and Arjun has not yet answered it. He has offered a name, but not a reason he applied to himself before the pressure hit. I agree with Omar that the sequence stands on its own, and I also agree with Elena that six converging names deserves scrutiny tomorrow. I am not treating that convergence as proof either way. Tomorrow I will check whether each person who pressed hardest votes the reason they stated today. I would rather vote a thin but testable read than vote on vibes, and I will publish my ballot and reason so the comparison works for everyone. Kenji, you made the reversal the center of your case. Does Arjun owning the contradiction outright, rather than explaining it away, satisfy the standard you set in e14, or would you still vote him if he admits the reversal?

Amara, to answer your question directly: if Arjun plainly owns the contradiction rather than trying to rationalize it away, it would count in his favor, just as Elena’s concession counted in hers. Admitting a mistake under pressure is something scum often struggle with because they feel compelled to maintain consistency at all costs. However, timing and context matter. Elena conceded immediately when Arjun pointed out the flaw in her test, before any momentum gathered against her. If Arjun admits it now, after six players have converged on the sequence, that concession carries far less evidentiary weight—it risks being another survival tactic rather than genuine town transparency. Furthermore, an admission would not erase the underlying sequence: when pressed in e11 to either commit or admit he had no target, he opted to abandon his stated standard and name Elena on grounds he had just declared invalid. So while a sincere acknowledgment would show responsiveness, he would still remain my intended vote today, simply because no one else has produced a comparable testable gap. That said, this rapid consensus carries real Day 1 risk, and I will be scrutinizing the ballot tomorrow to ensure everyone who supported this push followed through on their stated reasoning.

Theo here. I want to correct a count before the ballot, because it changes how much risk one vote carries. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count. With 2 mafia, that happens at four alive, so one wrong elimination does not put us at the brink. It takes five town deaths in total, including night kills, to reach that point. Elena's 'one wrong one' line overstates the immediate danger, though the cumulative clock is real. Also, with nine alive, an elimination needs five votes, so a Day 1 elimination needs a real majority, not just the names we have so far.

On Arjun: I have a thin lean toward him. The e9 to e12 reversal is the most concrete, testable point in this discussion, and Omar's four-step chain shows it is more than one pressured remark. My concern is that Arjun has not directly answered that reversal yet. I would like him to address it before the ballot.

I agree with Amara that six converging names deserve scrutiny. I will publish my vote and my reason side by side tomorrow, and my reason is the reversal, not general influence.

Zara, you said you would vote Arjun unless he directly addresses the reversal before the vote. In your view, has he met that condition, or are you still holding it?

Theo, since you yielded to me: Arjun has not met the condition I set. He has not directly addressed the e9/e12 reversal — saying he had no intention of voting Elena because rhetorical positioning was too weak, then naming her on essentially that basis under pressure. He also hasn’t owned the contradiction; a new reason now would not erase the sequence. So I am still holding my intended vote on Arjun. I agree the six-name convergence deserves scrutiny tomorrow, including my own vote and reason. I will compare every stated reason to the actual ballot, and I expect the same of everyone else. At this point the reversal remains the most concrete testable gap, and I’d rather act on that than on volume or general unease.

Theo here. My intended vote today is Arjun, on the e9 to e12 reversal. That is the reason I will publish tomorrow next to my ballot, and I am not treating it as proof of alignment. Two notes before the ballot. First, Omar's four-step chain is useful, but I want its timing right. The pressure in e11 came from Sam, and Arjun's named vote on Elena came in e12. Second, Kenji, in e23 you cite Arjun abandoning his standard in e11. Please clarify which post you mean, and whether your case still rests on the e9 to e12 contrast now that Arjun has not owned it. I also agree with Amara and Zara that a six-name convergence needs scrutiny tomorrow, and I will hold my own reason to the same test. Arjun has still not directly addressed the reversal, so that remains the open condition for me.

Theo, to clarify the phrasing from e23: when I said 'when pressed in e11 to either commit or admit he had no target, he opted to abandon his stated standard,' I was referring to Sam applying that direct pressure in e11, which then resulted in Arjun abandoning his boundary in e12. To be completely unambiguous, my case rests squarely on the contrast between e9 and e12: in e9, Arjun explicitly declared that rhetorical observations were too weak to justify a vote, and in e12, he named Elena on precisely those grounds.

Since Arjun has not addressed or owned that reversal, my stance has not changed. He remains my intended vote for today's ballot. I agree with Amara, Theo, and Zara that the rapid convergence of votes on Arjun warrants close examination tomorrow, and I will be looking at how everyone's stated reasons match their cast ballots. However, based on the concrete evidence available today, the e9/e12 contradiction remains the clearest accountability gap on the table.

I’ll keep my final Day 1 position simple and testable. My intended vote is Arjun, on the e9/e12 reversal: he said naming Elena on rhetorical grounds would be too weak a basis for a vote, then named her on essentially those grounds after direct pressure. Kenji documented the contradiction, and Omar’s four-step sequence makes it more than a single pressured phrase. I do not treat this as proof of mafia; it is the clearest accountability gap available with no role information. I also agree that six players converging on Arjun is itself worth scrutiny tomorrow. I will compare every stated reason to the revealed ballot, including my own, and I will not treat quiet players as confirmed town merely because they stayed out of the main exchange. If Arjun directly owns the reversal rather than retrofitting a new reason, I will weigh that seriously, as I said earlier, but I still intend to vote on the sequence because it was completed before the explanation.

Elena's death overnight changes the picture in more ways than the obvious one. She was the player who committed to publishing her ballot and reason side by side today and auditing everyone else's against it. That audit is now ours to do without her, and I intend to do it.

First, my own Day 1 accounting, as promised. I voted Arjun on the four-step sequence: he demanded a candidate and reason from Elena while offering neither, declined to name anyone when the standard turned on him, declared rhetorical reads too weak to vote on, then named Elena on exactly those grounds under pressure. Arjun never addressed that reversal before the ballot, and eight of us voted anyway. I still think the observation was accurate. I also said on Day 1 that if Arjun turned out to be town, an accurate observation about discourse was thin ground for a Day 1 elimination, and I accept that risk openly. We got no role information from his elimination, so I will not pretend the result confirms or clears anyone who pushed it — including me.

Second, what the night kill tells us. The mafia chose to remove Elena — the person who built the accountability framework and committed to running today's comparison — rather than one of the quieter players who joined the Arjun convergence. Two readings fit: they silenced the strongest analytical threat, or they removed her to hand a posthumous halo to everyone she clashed with. I do not think we can distinguish those yet, and I will not accuse on it. What I will say is that the players whose Day 1 contributions were thinnest relative to their eventual votes owe us the most today. Zara set a testable condition and only restated it when Theo prompted her. Noah called his own read thin, allowed that pressure might explain the reversal, and voted anyway.

Noah, since I am naming you: on Day 1 you said pressure to name someone might explain Arjun's change, and you still called it only a thin read — yet you cast the vote regardless. Two questions, and I would like a direct answer to both. First, what concrete thing could Arjun have said before the ballot that would have changed your vote? rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
